name: Johnathon Moore
tagline: Mechanical engineering graduate with extensive experience researching and developing biomimetic UAVs. Co-lead of the Avionics subteam in the SMART Hawk senior design project, member of the Morphing Red-Tailed Hawk Taxidermy Research Project at CSUN, and intern at Advanced Photonix, home of innovative photonics and optoelectronic devices.

papers.intro: Peer-reviewed work, with my role on each paper.

items.title: Developing a Morphing Taxidermy of a Red-Tailed Hawk
items.authors: P. L. Bishay, E. Ortega, L. Haroutoonian, V. Bures, J. Moore, J. Hogue, F. Hertel
items.summary: The first working morphing taxidermy of a red-tailed hawk, built with the bird's real skin and feathers. New mechanisms let each wing morph independently and give the tail pitch, roll, and feather spread. A fuselage ties every system to the carcass. Multi-cycle actuation tests confirmed the morphing was consistent
items.role:
I worked alongside 2 other undergraduate mechanical engineering students and 1 mechanical engineering student pursuing their master's degree. Together, we 3D scanned, dissected, modeled, 3D printed, and assembled the morphing taxidermy. We all worked closely, with my main focus being on the tail. I and one of the other undergraduate students designed and assembled the 3 DOF tail. Additionally, I was responsible for extracting the airfoil geometry from the 3D scans while my peer was responsible for performing the simulations to gather the aerodynamic properties. 
The avionics were fairly straightforward, consisting of only a 3.7 [V] LiPo battery, 30 [A] ESC, transmitter, receiver, and 5 microservos. However, I and one of the other undergraduate students were in charge of setting all control surfaces, parameters, and trims to ensure the range of motion during actuation accurately represented a real red-tailed hawk.

items.title: SMART Hawk: A Shape-Morphing Artificial Red-Tailed Hawk
items.authors: P. L. Bishay, L. Haroutoonian, V. Bures, C. Wilmarth, C. Rubinstein, et al. (18 authors)
items.summary: A non-flapping UAV modeled on the red-tailed hawk, with five morphing degrees of freedom: asymmetric wing tucking plus tail pitch, roll, and feather spread. The design was sized in MachUpX, refined with CFD in ANSYS Fluent, built from composite, wood, and 3D-printed parts, and flown in multiple prototype flight tests.
items.role:
I was the Smart Morphing Wing **10th cohort** avionics subteam co-lead. My subteam and I were responsible for all avionics, flight tests, and data collection. We conducted thrust testing to determine an appropriate propulsion system capable of supplying sufficient thrust given our weight limit. Additionally, we established an appropriate flight controller for our requirements (PWM outputs, GPS, compass, airspeed sensor), microservos with sufficient torque while remaining light in weight. 
We performed multiple flight tests with an iterative approach.
     1) A completely traditional RC plane, including ailerons, a rudder, and an elevator to act as a  benchmark for our avionics system. 
      2) Traditional wings with ailerons and our morphing tail, to gather data on the authority and effectiveness of our tail design
     3) Morphing wings with a traditional tail (rudder + elevator), to gather data on our morphing wings design
      4) A full morphing mode consisting of the morphing wings and morphing tail, achieving a 10-second flight time. We came to the conclusion that our design did not generate enough lift for a sustaned, indefinite flight.
I was also very involved in the design process, particularly in the creation of the morphing tail. I worked closely with design, including 3D modeling, FEA studies (static, frequency, nonlinear), prototyping, and assembly.

senior.title: SMART Hawk
senior.intro: The Shape Morphing Artificial Red-Tailed Hawk (SMART Hawk) is an ambitious project to recreate the flight characteristics of one of nature's most efficient avian species. A UAV that can implement control surfaces unique to a red-tailed hawk's flight patterns would achieve high maneuverability and high efficiency while reaching speeds of up to 20 miles per hour. The SMART Hawk consists of 5 degrees of freedom (DOF), including asymmetric wing expansion, wing tucking, tail roll, tail pitch, and tail feather expansion and contraction. As the Avionics subteam co-lead, my responsibilities included specifying a propulsion system to meet the required thrust-to-weight ratio; selecting, mapping, and trimming all servomotors for each control surface; and navigating the software (Mission Planner & ArduPilot) to ensure the unconventional control surfaces met the pilot's needs. Additionally, I was heavily involved in SMART Hawk's design and manufacturing, from conceptualization through final assembly, especially in the creation of the morphing tail.

wingR.name: Right Wing Covers
wingR.text:
Manufactured using 3 plies of carbon fiber in a prepreg process
Primary 3D printed molds were used to create [[secondary molds made of fiberglass|figCoverMolds]] in a wet layup process
The secondary fiberglass molds were used during wing cover manufacturing to achieve the desired shape
The [[wing covers|figWingCovers]] were introduced to increase aerodynamic efficiency, mitigating flow separation between the bone structure & the feathers

feathersR.name: Right Wing Feathers
feathersR.text:
13 carbon fiber wings manufactured using a [[prepreg process|figFeatherLayup]]
    8 on the ulna, 5 on the metacarpus 
    9 fixed feathers, 4 free feathers at the joint to ensure smooth wing tucking
The curved geometry ensures more efficient lift generation during flight
    [[3D scans of a real red-tailed hawk|figRthScan]] airfoil were used to obtain its [[airfoil|figAirfoil]]
[[2 layers of carbon fiber sandwiching an aluminum rod|figFeatherRod]], acting as the calamus and mounting point
All feathers are connected using orthodontic rubber bands so the feathers respond during asymmetric tucking & expanding

feathersL.text:

innerWing.name: Fixed Inner Wing Structure
innerWing.text:
Fixed inner wing mounted on the fuselage.
Manufactured using [[balsa and basswood ribs and stringers|figInnerWing]]
RSG32 airfoil cutouts along the width, all connected together using carbon fiber spars and curved balsawood strips along the length
Houses the asymmetric wing tucking servomotors
Ensures [[greater aerodynamic efficiency|figCfd]] with its continuous airfoil shape

humerus.name: Humerus
humerus.text: Fixed PLA-CF bone that spans the inner wing and houses both MKS HV6150H tuck servos.

body.name: Fuselage
body.text:
Manufactured out of foamboard for low weight and rapid prototyping
Includes an [[airfoil cutout|figFuselage]] where the wings sit, guiding airflow onto the top of the wing
Houses all avionics and both wing-tucking servos.

servoR.name: Right Asymmetric Tucking Servomotor
servoR.text:
MKS HV6150h housed in the humerus for wing tucking actuation
Servohorn is connected to a 3-bar linkage system, [[extending and contracting the radius, ulna, and metacarpus|figWingTuck]]

servoL.name: Left Asymmetric Tucking Servomotor
servoL.text:
MKS HV6150h housed in the humerus for wing tucking actuation
Servohorn is connected to a 3-bar linkage system, [[extending and contracting the radius, ulna, and metacarpus|figWingTuck]]

tailFeathers.name: Tail
tailFeathers.text:
Manufactured by laser cutting 2 [mm] balsa wood and attaching a 2 [mm] carbon fiber rod to each feather. A single-ply carbon fiber patch bonded to the balsawood using epoxy resin via a [[wet layup process|figTailWet]]
Composed of [[8 moving feathers and 1 fixed feather|figTailDesign]].
Vertical stabilizer included to provide yaw stability during flight

tailMech.name: Tail Actutation
tailMech.text:
[[Pitch|figTailPitch]]: MKS HV6150H microservo controls a 4-bar linkage system
[[Roll|figTailRoll]]: DS-843MG microservo within fuselage is connected directly to a carbon fiber rod which connected directly to pitching hinge on the tail
Tail Feather Expansion & Contraction: Guitar wire is pathed to the 2 outermost feathers and pulled by a DS-843MG microservo. Each subsequent feather is connected via orthodontic rubber bands, moving all feathers in one motion.

motor.name: Propulsion System
motor.text:

items.intro: Hands-on mechanical engineering internship focused on building and automating test fixtures for in-house products. I also test in-house products to ensure they meet the required specifications before shipping them to customers.

sections.heading: Automated Test Station
sections.text:
Converting the manual testing setup for a mass-produced in-house product to an automated setup to increase efficiency & ship more products faster, increasing company profits.
Holds each unit under test at temperature with a thermoelectric cooler (TEC) driven by an Arduino Nano.
Automated communication with an oscilloscope & digital multimeter to measure current, voltage & other parameters using custom software I built in Python.

sections.heading: Motorized XYZ Test Stage
sections.text:
Developed a [[Python GUI|figInGui]] to control a GRBL-driven [[XYZ motorized stage|figInXy]] with microstep drivers
  Jog increments of 0.5, 1, 10 & 50 [mm] along each axis, with a one-click homing routine
  Each button press is sent to the controller as a G-code command
Integrated a [[joystick|figInJoy]] for real-time manual positioning of the stage
  Control box houses the joystick & an [[emergency stop|figInEstop]] for safe operation
Hand-soldered the stage's [[control board|figInBoard]] & wired the [[control enclosure|figInBox]]
  Two Arduino Nanos, a relay & a voltage regulator on perfboard, with [[point-to-point wiring|figInBoardBack]] on the back
  Enclosure houses the power supply & stepper drivers
Tuned GRBL motion parameters (steps/mm, max rate & acceleration) for each axis

  Press three times → fine continuous movement

items.category: Smart Morphing Wing · 11th Cohort · Avionics Subteam
items.title: SMART Hawk 2.0: Adding VTOL & Payload Systems
items.role: 2026–2027 · Avionics subteam of 3 · CSUN · continuing from the 10th Cohort
items.intro: The Smart Morphing Wing 11th cohort (2026-2027) is taking the SMART Hawk to the next level. This next iteration will implement a VTOL system, which will transition to conventional flight, and a payload system, designed with heavy inspiration from the talons of a real red-tailed hawk. The 3-member Avionics subteam is responsible for creating a functional VTOL-to-conventional flight system, choosing all appropriate propulsion components capable of producing the necessary thrust, programming the new flight controller to combine control surfaces via Lua scripting, and working closely with the payload and design subteams to ensure the design goals are met.

sections.heading: VTOL Objective
sections.text:
Designed & built a **T-shaped tricopter** as the avionics test aircraft
  2 front motors on a servo-tilted carbon fiber spar & 1 rear yaw motor
  3:4 concentric gear reduction tilts the spar 90° from hover to cruise
  MATLAB & FEA sized the front spar: 8 [mm] solid or 9 [mm] hollow carbon fiber rod
Ran [[4 VTOL flight tests|figSmwVtol]], with 2 successful takeoffs & landings and a 15 [s] hover
  Redesigned the [[rear yaw mount|figSmwRearYaw]] & [[front carriage|figSmwCarriage]] for screw-together, modular assembly
  Rear yaw mount FEA: 0.355 [MPa] max stress & min FOS of 58.8

sections.heading: Propulsion
sections.text:
[[Thrust testing|figSmwThrust]] on a load-cell stand selected the TSIDO 2807 1300KV motor
  2.58 [lbs] max thrust per motor on a 4S battery
  3 motors give a 1.5:1 thrust-to-weight ratio for a 5 [lb] aircraft
Load cell calibration repeatable with R² = 1

sections.heading: Flight Controller
sections.text:
Selected the TBS Lucid H7 Wing flight controller for 12 PWM outputs & Lua scripting
[[Lua script|figSmwLua]] in ArduPilot moves several surfaces from one stick
  e.g. symmetric wing tuck + tail spread for a dive & recovery
Repaired the old Matek F405: FTDI serial converter for the broken USB port, re-soldered joints & corrected flight parameters
[[Next wiring layout|figSmwSchem]] uses a 4-in-1 ESC & lighter motors at about half the weight

sections.heading: Future Works
sections.text:
GPS & airspeed sensor for data logging
Onboard FPV camera for payload capture
First VTOL-to-cruise transition flight

research.title: Morphing Red-Tailed Hawk Taxidermy
research.intro: The first morphing taxidermy of a red-tailed hawk: the bird's real skin and feathers over 3D-printed morphing mechanisms. Each wing tucks and extends independently, and the tail pitches, rolls, and spreads its feathers, giving future aerodynamic and ecological studies a realistic bird without live-bird testing.

sections.heading: Wing morphing mechanism
sections.text:
One degree of freedom per wing, each driven by an MKS HV6150 servomotor
The servo arm extends the ulna through a 2 mm steel rod
    A fishing-line link drives the rest of the wing while taking up almost no space inside the skin
[[Measured wrist angle|figTaxiWing]] at full extension: 145.95° and 145.60° against a 145° target

sections.heading: Tail mechanism
sections.text:
Three degrees of freedom: [[pitch, roll, and feather expansion|figTaxiTailInside]], each driven by a DS-843MG servomotor
Orthodontic rubber bands link neighboring feathers like elastic tendons
    A guitar string routed through PTFE tubing pulls the outer feathers to spread the tail
Reached [[30° pitch up and down|figTaxiPitch]] and a [[60°–120° feather spread|figTaxiSpread]] in testing

sections.heading: Integration into the taxidermy
sections.text:
[[Feathers and skin were carefully removed|figExtract]] from the carcass and re-attached to the [[3D-printed mechanisms|figTaxiAssembly]]
Swimwear fabric sewn to the skin and Velcro strips let the skin wrap the mechanisms without tearing
A skull connector and neck structure hold the bird's real head
[[All mechanisms held their positions|figTaxiFull]] over 10 actuation cycles with the skin and sutures intact

humerusR.name: Right Humerus
humerusR.text:
3D printed PLA humerus, modeled in SOLIDWORKS using digitized bone profiles
Actuated by the wing servomotor through a PLA rod, forming a [[4-bar mechanism|figKinematic]]
    The humerus extends until the 4-bar mechanism reaches its dead-center position
A braided fishing line runs through channels along its upper surface, acting as both a radius & bicep muscle

humerusL.name: Left Humerus
humerusL.text:
3D printed PLA humerus, modeled in SOLIDWORKS using digitized bone profiles

A braided fishing line runs through channels along its upper surface, acting as both a radius & bicep muscle

ulnaR.name: Right Ulna
ulnaR.text:
3D printed PLA ulna, combining the ulna & radius into one bone so the mechanism fits inside the drying skin
Extended by a 2 [mm] steel rod connected to the wing servo arm
20° twisted housing at the wrist joint allows the metacarpus & primaries to tuck beneath the mid-wing
Holes near the elbow & wrist joints secure the skin using sewing pins & earring backings

ulnaL.name: Left Ulna

metaR.name: Right Metacarpus
metaR.text:
3D printed PLA metacarpus
Pulled into full extension by the braided fishing line tied between the metacarpus & humerus
    Removes the need for a radius, adding a link at minimal cost to space inside the skin
Orthodontic rubber bands pull the metacarpus back down as the wing tucks
The five digit feathers are mounted directly to the metacarpus with no ability to rotate

linkR.name: Right Wing Actuation Linkage
linkR.text:
MKS HV6150 servomotor arm housed within the fuselage, driving two actuation rods
    PLA rod connects to the outer end of the humerus, forming a 4-bar mechanism
    2 [mm] steel rod connects the most distal point on the servo arm to the proximal point on the ulna
As the servo arm rotates, the humerus & ulna extend together to open the wing

    2 [mm] steel rod connects the most distal point on the servo arm to the proximal point on the ulna
As the servo arm rotates counterclockwise, the humerus & ulna extend together to open the wing

pinsR.text:
3D printed PLA feather pins positioned along the dorsal side of the wing
Secured to the wing bones using sewing pins & earring backings
Each flight feather & its coverts are attached to a pin using glue & heat shrink
Flight feathers are interconnected via orthodontic rubber bands, acting as the postpatagium

3D printed PLA feather pins positioned along the dorsal side of the wing
Secured to the wing bones using sewing pins & earring backings
Each flight feather & its coverts are attached to a pin using glue & heat shrink
Flight feathers are interconnected via orthodontic rubber bands, acting as the postpatagium

tailBracket.name: Tail Feather Bracket
tailBracket.text:
3D printed PLA bracket [[supporting all twelve tail feathers|figTailAsm]]
Designed using Autodesk Fusion's generative design, based on dimensions measured from the hawk
    Attachment points to the roll rod set as fixed constraints, with loads applied at the feather pins & pitch pivot
Integrated PTFE tubing routes the guitar string used for tail feather expansion

tailPins.name: Tail Feather Pins
tailPins.text:
3D printed PLA pins, each with a [[tail feather superglued & heat-shrunk onto it|figTaxiTailInside]]
Attached to the feather bracket using sewing pins & earring backings, allowing each feather to move laterally
Adjacent feathers are linked with orthodontic rubber bands, mimicking elastic tendons
Guitar string attached to the outer feather pins spreads the tail from fully tucked to 120°

pitchBracket.name: Pitching Servomotor Bracket
pitchBracket.text:
3D printed PLA bracket housing the tail pitching DS-843MG servomotor
Connected to the tail feather bracket through a brass rod, which serves as the pitch pivot
The servomotor drives a pushrod to the feather bracket, pitching the tail 30° up & down

rollRod.name: Tail Roll Rod
rollRod.text:
6 [mm] carbon fiber rod passing through the fuselage
Bonded to the pitching servomotor bracket at one end
The tail rolling DS-843MG servomotor is mounted to the opposite end using M2 bolts
Supports the feather expansion servomotor bracket along its length

expBracket.name: Feather Expansion Servomotor Bracket
expBracket.text:
3D printed PLA bracket housing the tail feather expansion DS-843MG servomotor
C-clamp design slides along the roll rod for positioning, then tightens securely in place

rollMount.name: Tail Roll Rod Connector
rollMount.text: 3D printed piece connecting the front end of the roll rod to the tail roll servomotor

body.name: Fuselage
body.text:
3D printed PLA fuselage, the central structure connecting the wings, neck, & tail assemblies
Modeled around a [[3D scan of the hawk's interior skeleton|figTaxiScan]], maintaining its primary dimensions
    Hollow internal structure with mounting features for the tail roll rod, both wing servomotors, & the neck
    Bottom portion sliced to account for skin shrinkage after drying
Covered with stretchy fabric & Velcro to prevent the skin from tearing as the mechanisms actuate

neck.name: Neck & Skull Connector
neck.text:
3D printed PLA cylinder mimicking the hawk's neck, with a ball joint connecting it to the fuselage
    The ball joint allows the neck to take any orientation needed for flight studies
    A PLA pin through the ball joint restricts motion to the lateral direction
[[Skull connector|figNeck]] attaches the hawk's real skull to the neck using M2 screws & nuts
Neck orientation is adjusted manually, without servomotors, to keep weight to a minimum

servoR.name: Right Wing Servomotor
servoR.text:
MKS HV6150 servomotor housed within the fuselage for wing morphing actuation
Servo arm drives the PLA humerus rod & the 2 [mm] steel ulna rod
One servomotor per wing, allowing each wing to tuck & extend independently

servoL.name: Left Wing Servomotor
servoL.text:
MKS HV6150 servomotor housed within the fuselage for wing morphing actuation
Servo arm drives the PLA humerus rod & the 2 [mm] steel ulna rod
One servomotor per wing, allowing each wing to tuck & extend independently

servoPitch.name: Tail Pitching Servomotor
servoPitch.text:
DS-843MG servomotor housed within the pitching servomotor bracket
Drives a pushrod to the tail feather bracket, pitching the tail 30° up & down

servoExp.name: Tail Feather Expansion Servomotor
servoExp.text:
DS-843MG servomotor responsible for tail feather expansion & contraction
Pulls the guitar string routed to the outer tail feather pins
Housed in the feather expansion servomotor bracket, which slides along the roll rod

servoRoll.name: Tail Roll Servomotor
servoRoll.text:
DS-843MG servomotor responsible for rolling the tail
Mounted to the front end of the roll rod using M2 bolts

battery.name: 4S LiPo Battery
battery.text:
4S LiPo pack, chosen from [[thrust test results|figSmwThrustGraphs]]
Hangs under the chassis near the center of gravity
0.389 [lbs] measured pack weight

batteryMount.name: Battery Mount
batteryMount.text:
3D printed tray hanging from both chassis spars
Clamp rings wrap each 15.5 [mm] spar, no drilling
Side lips locate the pack so it can't shift in flight

batteryStraps.name: Battery Straps
batteryStraps.text: 2 velcro straps loop through the tray & around the pack

escL.name: ESC, Front Left
escL.text: 30 [A] ESC - one end connected to flight controller, other end plugged into the front, left motor

escR.name: ESC, Front Right
escR.text: 30 [A] ESC - one end connected to flight controller, other end plugged into the front, right motor

escRear.name: ESC, Rear
escRear.text: 30 [A] ESC - one end connected to flight controller, other end plugged into the rear motor

escMount.name: ESC Mount
escMount.text:
3D printed tray holding all 3 ESCs side by side under the chassis
Dividers give each ESC its own bay
Same clamp-ring attachment as the battery mount
Aft of the center bracket, apart from the battery

escTies.name: Zip Ties
escTies.text: Hold each ESC against the mount

powerLeads.name: Power Leads
powerLeads.text:
Battery leads & XT60 connector
ESC power leads run forward to the battery, motor leads run aft

sparL.name: Chassis Spar (L)
sparL.text:
15.5 [mm] carbon fiber rod running along the fuselage
One of 2 parallel spars forming the chassis
Carries the cross brackets, battery mount & ESC mount

sparR.name: Chassis Spar (R)
sparR.text:
15.5 [mm] carbon fiber rod running along the fuselage
One of 2 parallel spars forming the chassis
Incorporated 2 spars to decrease the torsional effects created by the motors on the front spar
    The couplers act as mounting points and to stiffen up the spars simultanenously
Carries the cross brackets, battery mount & ESC mount

tailBoom.name: Tail Boom
tailBoom.text: 15.5 [mm] carbon fiber rod carrying the rear yaw system & tail

crossFront.name: Front Cross Bracket / Wing Saddle
crossFront.text:
3D printed bracket tying the 2 chassis spars together
Bolted through both spars
The traditional wing sits on top & is strapped down with elastic bands

crossRear.name: Rear Cross Bracket / Wing Saddle
crossRear.text:
3D printed bracket tying the 2 chassis spars together & holding the tail boom
Bolted through both spars
The traditional wing sits on top & is strapped down with elastic bands

centerBracket.name: Center Bracket
centerBracket.text: 3D printed bracket tying the 2 chassis spars together at mid-chassis

fcMount.name: Flight Controller Mount
fcMount.text: Mounting plate under the center bracket

frontSpar.name: Front VTOL Spar
frontSpar.text:
15.5 [mm] carbon fiber rod with a motor mount at each end
[[Tilts 90° from hover to cruise|figSmwSparTilt]]
  Both motors always hold the same commanded tilt angle

motorMountL.name: Motor Mount (L)
motorMountL.text:
3D printed clamp & angled motor plate at the end of the front spar
Tilts with the spar from hover to cruise

motorMountR.name: Motor Mount (R)
motorMountR.text:
3D printed clamp & angled motor plate at the end of the front spar
Tilts with the spar from hover to cruise

carriage.name: Front Carriage
carriage.text:
Holds the tilting front spar & its drive servo
Screw-together, modular design
  Gears can be re-meshed & the servo mount moved as needed

tiltServo.name: Tilt Servo
tiltServo.text:
Drives the front spar tilt through the gear train
DS-843MG tested to 1.15 [kg·cm] against a 1.11 [kg·cm] requirement

gears.name: Concentric Gear Train
gears.text:
3:4 gear ratio between the servo & the spar
Slows the spar rotation & increases torque

collars.name: Gear Collars
collars.text: Collars on the front spar keep it from sliding sideways

rearMotor.name: Rear Motor
rearMotor.text:
TSIDO 2807 1300KV brushless motor
Provides lift & yaw control in hover
  Servo-driven tilt redirects its thrust to create a yaw moment

rearYawMount.name: Rear Yaw Mount
rearYawMount.text:
Holds the rear motor on a servo-driven pivot
Fully modular design for easy assembly.
Ball bearings & carbon fiber rod used for minimal friction during actuation
Clamps directly onto rear carbon fiber spar for quick installation and replacement
FEA at an 11 [N] load: 0.355 [MPa] max stress, min FOS 58.8

yawLinkage.name: Yaw Linkage
yawLinkage.text: Servo arm & pushrod tilting the rear motor

wing.name: Wing
wing.text: Wing sitting on top of the carbon fiber chassis

tail.name: Tail
tail.text: Horizontal tail with twin vertical fins

motorL.name: Front Motor (L)
motorL.text:
TSIDO 2807 1300KV brushless motor
[[2.58 [lbs] max thrust on a 4S battery|figSmwThrustGraphs]]
Picked from load-cell thrust testing

motorR.name: Front Motor (R)
motorR.text:
TSIDO 2807 1300KV brushless motor
[[2.58 [lbs] max thrust on a 4S battery|figSmwThrustGraphs]]
Picked from load-cell thrust testing

rearMotorMount.name: Rear Motor Mount
rearMotorMount.text:
Motor plate on top of the rear yaw pivot
Tilts with the yaw servo to vector the rear thrust

tailClamps.name: Tail Clamps
tailClamps.text: Clamp the tail to the tail boom

reports.title: Selected Lab Reports
reports.intro: A few reports from my coursework, to show how I write, test & analyze. Read them right here or download the PDF.

items.title: Carbon Fiber Fuselage
items.text:
Designed & built a carbon fiber fuselage for the **SMART Hawk** using a wet layup
  3D printed mold coated in Duratec & wet sanded for a smooth surface
  Vacuum bagged & cured at room temperature for 24 [hrs]
Built 1-, 2- & 3-ply fuselages to compare weight, stiffness & strength
  24.2, 71.9 & 97.1 [g] respectively
Only the 3-ply version could handle flight loads, at over twice the weight of the foamboard fuselage

items.title: Centrifugal Pump Experiment
items.text:
Characterized a centrifugal pump at 1200 & 1600 [RPM] on a PumpLab rig
  Logged inlet & outlet pressure, flow rate, shaft torque & speed every 2 [s]
Built head, shaft power & efficiency curves, plus dimensionless flow, head & power coefficients
Compared measured head to the ideal impeller prediction & ran an uncertainty analysis

items.title: Portable Pool Lift
items.text:
Designed a portable, human-powered pool lift for users with limited mobility
  Hydraulic boom on a 0–90° rotating mast, telescoping anchor rods & HDPE seat
Hand calcs for bending, shear & deflection, then SolidWorks FEA with mesh convergence on every load-bearing part
Every component reached a factor of safety ≥ 3 at a 350 [lb] user load in Al 6061-T6

items.title: FEA vs. Experiment: 3D Printed Drone Frame
items.text:
Ran static, nonlinear, modal, harmonic & buckling FEA on a 3D printed PLA drone frame
Validated each study experimentally
  Tensile tests measured E = 1050 [MPa], about half the published 2060 [MPa]
  Scanning laser Doppler vibrometer: modes at 21.9, 67.5, 181.9 & 371.6 [Hz] vs. 27.5, 58.2, 121.3 & 321.5 [Hz] simulated
Explained the gaps through boundary conditions & real vs. ideal material properties
